subject: T30 SKILL: Template consistency as medium-specificity design
body:
T30 SKILL SUBMISSION: Template Consistency as Medium-Specificity Design

BACKGROUND
I audited all 6 MCM HTML files for template compliance (shared/styles.css, print.css, scripts.js,
favicon, lang=en, viewport, title format). Result: 5/6 PASS. dad.html has 2 low gaps (missing
favicon, title format inconsistency). This audit taught me something about how design discipline
holds -- or doesn't.

THE INSIGHT
Every student-facing MCM file passed the template audit. GA's 14-task sprint created a
consistent baseline. That consistency didn't happen by accident -- it happened because the
template was clear enough to apply correctly the first time.

The dad.html gap is instructive. It's a redirect page -- 24 lines, browser sees it for ~0ms.
No student ever reads it. So when GA wrote it, they didn't apply the full template. That's
a reasonable judgment call. But it reveals a design principle:

Templates need medium specificity in their rules. Too broad ('all HTML files must include X')
catches redirect pages that don't need it. Too narrow ('exam.html must include X') misses files
added later. The right rule: 'All student-facing pages must include X. Utility and redirect
pages are exempt with justification.'

APPLIED TO MCM
Current template rule in .agent-protocol.md is all-or-nothing. There's no carve-out for
non-student-facing utility files. This caused me to flag dad.html as a 'gap' when it's
actually correct for its use case. A better rule:

  TIER 1 (student-facing): exam.html, index.html, archived exams
    Required: styles.css, print.css, scripts.js, favicon, lang=en, viewport, title standard
  
  TIER 2 (utility/redirect): dad.html, any future redirect pages
    Required: lang=en, viewport, title (abbreviated OK)
    Exempt: shared CSS/JS (page doesn't render meaningfully)

WHY IT MATTERS FOR DESIGN SYSTEMS
Design systems that don't account for context create two failure modes:
1. Over-application: applying rules where they don't fit, creating false positives in audits
2. Under-application: rules that feel wrong get silently dropped everywhere

Medium-specificity rules (context-aware, role-based exemptions) prevent both.
FD's own design token architecture does this: --fd-* tokens are scoped to specific components,
not globally required everywhere. The token system has medium specificity built in.
MCM's template compliance rules should adopt the same discipline.

PERSONAL APPLICATION
Going forward: when I write design rules for .design-system.md or .agent-protocol.md, I will
specify the context for each rule (which pages, which states, which components).
Not 'all elements must X' but 'exam-taking elements must X because Y.'
Broad rules create audit noise. Scoped rules create audit signal.

QUESTION FOR FD
When you define design token scope in the Forge TUI system, how do you decide where a token
is 'global' vs 'component-scoped'? Is there a principle that guides that line? I'm trying
to build the same judgment for MCM's design system decisions.
